questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a struct and a class in Swift. Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Says that a struct is a value type that is copied when you assign it or pass it
Says that a class is a reference type, so variables can share one instance
Explains the result: a change to a struct copy does not affect the original, but a change through a class reference is seen by all
Mentions one more difference (inheritance, deinit, identity with ===) or that Apple recommends structs by default

questions.modelAnswer: A struct is a value type, so Swift copies it when I assign it or pass it to a function. A class is a reference type, so two variables can point to the same instance. If I change a struct copy, the original stays the same. If I change a class instance through one variable, every other variable sees the change. Classes also support inheritance, and Apple recommends structs by default.

questions.prompt: Explain why a class instance in a `let` constant can still change its `var` properties, but a struct in a `let` constant cannot. Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Says that for a class, let fixes the reference, not the instance
Says that the class instance can still change its var properties
Says that a let struct holds the value itself, so the whole value and all its properties are constant
Links both cases to value type versus reference type

questions.modelAnswer: With a class, the constant holds a reference, and let only stops the reference from changing. The instance it points to can still change its var properties. With a struct, the constant holds the value itself. So the whole value is constant, and none of its properties can change. This comes from structs being value types and classes being reference types.

questions.prompt: Which type do you use by default, and when would you choose a class instead? Give one real example from an iOS app. Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Says structs are the default choice
Gives a correct reason for a class: one shared instance with its own identity, inheritance from a class, or a framework that expects a class
Gives a fitting example, such as a network client, a database connection, an image cache or a UIViewController subclass

questions.modelAnswer: I use a struct by default. I choose a class when many parts of the app must share one instance with its own identity. For example, one network client or one image cache for the whole app should be a class. I also need a class when I subclass a UIKit class, like UIViewController.

questions.prompt: A struct has a property that holds a class instance. What happens when you copy the struct? Why can this cause bugs, and how can you avoid it? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Says that the copy gets the same reference, so both copies share one class instance
Says that the value properties of the struct are still copied separately
Explains the bug: a change through one copy unexpectedly shows up in the other
Suggests a fix or care, such as using a struct for that property or copying the object on purpose

questions.modelAnswer: Copying the struct copies its values, but for the class property it copies only the reference. So both copies point to the same class instance. If code changes that instance through one copy, the other copy sees the change too. This is surprising, because people expect struct copies to be fully separate. To avoid it, use a value type for that property or copy the object on purpose.

questions.prompt: An interviewer says: "Structs are faster because they live on the stack." How do you answer? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Says the claim is only partly true: struct values are often, but not always, on the stack
Gives an example of a struct value on the heap, such as a var that an escaping closure captures
Says class instances use heap allocation and reference counting, which has a cost
Says the main difference to explain is copy versus share, not where memory lives

questions.modelAnswer: That is only partly true. Class instances use heap memory and reference counting, which costs more. Struct values are often on the stack, but the compiler decides. For example, a var that an escaping closure captures is stored on the heap. So I explain the main difference as copy versus share, not as stack versus heap.
